Claude: The premise looks shaky, at least through mid-year. China's stock market has been choppy in 2026, but not clearly bad. I don't have data from the last few months, so it may have changed.

	•	Modest gains: The CSI 300 gained roughly 5% since the start of the year through mid-2026. 
	•	Highs, then pullbacks: In June the index hit its highest level since December 2021. By July 9 it had slipped to a one-month low.  
	•	Strong over 12 months: It was still up about 15% year over year in March. That follows a very strong 2025. 

It's more modest than the 2025 rally, and volatile. Some markets, like Hong Kong, may be weaker than mainland indices.

Do stocks reflect the economy? Only loosely, and China is a good example of why:

	•	Different drivers: Stocks respond to earnings, valuations, liquidity and sentiment. Chinese households have also put savings into equities amid falling bank deposit rates and a continuing slump in home prices. That means stocks can rise while the property sector, still a big part of household wealth, struggles. 
	•	Composition: Listed companies skew toward tech, finance and industrials, not the whole economy.
	•	Mixed signals now: Exports are booming, with a likely trade surplus near $1.2 trillion. But domestic consumption and property remain weak, and the 2026 growth target was lowered to 4.5–5%.

So a soft stock market and a strong export sector can coexist.
